analysis.one_liner: Gives federal regulators authority to set safety standards for and recall dangerous firearms and ammunition.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee from March 1999 until the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would treat guns, ammunition, and parts like other consumer products: the Treasury Secretary could write safety rules, order recalls, refunds, and repairs of dangerous models, fine violators up to $5,000 per product (rising to $10,000), allow consumers to sue, and maintain a public clearinghouse on firearm injuries. It would not preempt state gun laws and would not apply to government agencies. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and its Crime Subcommittee, where it died without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to defective or dangerously designed guns and ammunition. The bill would let regulators require recalls and refunds of defective firearms, require testing and labeling before sale, give shooting victims and other injured people the right to sue for damages with attorney's fees available, and create a public database on firearm deaths and injuries to help buyers compare products.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun owners, buyers, and shooting victims

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Treasury Secretary to write regulations governing the design, manufacture, and performance of firearms, ammunition, parts, and nonpowder guns where reasonably necessary to prevent unreasonable risk of injury [S2][S3].

Authorizes the Secretary to order manufacturers and dealers to warn the public, repair, replace, refund, or recall firearm products found defective or unreasonably risky, and to ban manufacture or sale of products that cannot be made safe [S2][S3].

Creates a private right to sue for damages for anyone injured by a violation, allows any interested person to sue to enforce the act, and lets courts award attorney's fees to prevailing plaintiffs [S2][S3].

Requires manufacturers to test and certify products, label them with manufacturer and importer identities, keep records open to federal inspection, and bans stockpiling products ahead of a new rule taking effect [S2][S3].
Requires the Treasury to run a public Firearm Injury Information Clearinghouse, study firearm deaths and injuries and their costs, and publish the results at least annually [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearms and ammunition manufacturers, importers, and dealers, who would bear testing, certification, labeling, record-keeping, recall, and refund costs and face civil fines, private lawsuits, and up to two years' imprisonment for knowing violations after notice. Consumers could pay more for guns if compliance costs were passed through, and some products found unreasonably risky could be banned from sale entirely.

drawbacks.text: The bill gives the Treasury Secretary broad power to ban outright the manufacture, import, transfer, distribution, or export of any firearm product deemed an unreasonable risk — potentially restricting access to widely owned firearms and ammunition, not just defective ones [S3].

Compliance costs for testing, certification, labeling, and records would be borne by manufacturers and dealers, including small gun shops and pawnbrokers (who are covered by the bill's definition of dealer), and could raise prices for buyers [S3].
Separately counting each product involved as a violation, with fines per product, exposes manufacturers to very large penalties for a single compliance lapse across a production run [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill applies a familiar consumer-product safety playbook — standards, recalls, labeling, research, and lawsuits — to firearms, which are currently the only major consumer product Congress has left outside a federal safety regulator's jurisdiction. The benefit is a systematic way to get defective and dangerous models off the market and give injured people recourse; the cost is compliance burdens on a legal industry and the possibility that broad ban authority could restrict lawfully owned guns. Whether the ban authority is a feature or a flaw depends on one's view of gun access, but the core recall-and-standards machinery is the same framework used for toys, appliances, and cars.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, which sent it to its Crime Subcommittee eight days later, and it sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Patrick J. Kennedy (D-RI) introduced the Firearms Safety and Consumer Protection Act of 1999 on March 2, 1999 [S1][S3][S5].
The House referred the bill to the Judiciary Committee the same day, and on March 10 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime [S5].
Twenty-eight House Democrats joined as cosponsors; no Republicans signed on [S4].
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a subcommittee vote, committee markup, or floor vote before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers and dealers are better off: they avoided safety standards, recall obligations, per-product fines, and the private lawsuits the bill would have created, and firearms remain outside any federal consumer-safety regime.

for.name: Rep. Patrick J. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and championed consumer-product-style safety regulation of firearms.

for.name: 28 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or brought the bill to the full committee after its referral.

against.name: Subcommittee on Crime
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 10, 1999 and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed regulation of firearms as consumer products, lobbying against bills that would subject guns to safety-regulator oversight.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 members of the House associated with the bill — the sponsor and 28 cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican support appears in the record [S4].

industries.industry: Firearms and ammunition manufacturers, importers, and dealers (including pawnbrokers)
industries.note: The bill would impose testing, certification, labeling, record-keeping, inspection, recall, and refund obligations on this industry, with fines per product and private lawsuits. Its interest in defeating the bill ran against consumers' interest in a recall system for defective and dangerously designed firearms. Firearms are the only major consumer product category excluded from federal consumer-product safety oversight, so the bill would have ended that exception.
